comment_box: The Reproductive Freedom Alliance (RFA) is pleased to submit the attached comments in response to the notice of proposed rulemaking entitled “Reproductive Health Services” published in the Federal Register on August 4, 2025 (RIN 2900-AS31). As a nonpartisan coalition of 23 governors, the RFA opposes all efforts to reduce access to necessary health care for our nation’s veterans. We are deeply concerned by the proposed rollback of reproductive health care access to which veterans, and their families, are entitled. We appreciate the opportunity to provide our input. Please do not hesitate to contact us with any questions.

===== FILE 20758__1.pdf =====
September 3rd, 2025 
 
VIA ELECTRONIC TRANSMISSION  
 
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins  
Secretary, U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Ave. NW  
Washington, DC 20420  
 
The Honorable Dr. Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health, Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Ave. NW,  
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Re: Comments on Reproductive Health Services (RIN 2900-AS31)  
 
Dear Secretary Collins and Acting Under Secretary Lieberman:  
 
The Reproductive Freedom Alliance (RFA) submits these comments in opposition to the U.S. 
Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposed rule entitled “Reproductive Health Services,” 
published in the Federal Register on August 4, 2025 (RIN 2900-AS31). As a nonpartisan 
coalition of 23 governors, the RFA opposes all efforts to reduce access to necessary health care 
for our nation’s veterans, who have served our country and fought to protect our fundamental 
freedoms, and their families.1  
Proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31 revokes the already-limited existing access to abortion care and 
counseling for veterans and their beneficiaries through the VA medical benefits package and the 
Civilian Health and Medical Program (CHAMPVA).2 Current rules at the VA currently limit 
abortion access to situations of rape, incest and where the life or health of the pregnant patient

Evers. 
2 Reproductive Health Services, Department of Veterans Affairs, 38 CFR Part 17 RIN 2900-
AS31 (2025). https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/04/2025-14687/reproductive-
health-services  

 
 
 
 
are at risk.3 The new proposed rule threatens the health and wellbeing of those who served our 
country by further restricting access only to cases where the patient’s life is threatened, and lacks 
clarity even as to those critically important situations, and eliminating access to counseling 
entirely. We are deeply concerned by the federal government’s proposed rollback of 
reproductive health care access to which veterans, and their families, are entitled.  
A. The proposed rule is extreme and will worsen health outcomes. 
Under the previous administration, the VA recognized that allowing abortion access through the 
VA medical benefits package and the CHAMPVA only for instances of life endangerment was 
too narrow and threatened veterans’ and their families’ health. In updating 38 CFR Part 17 to 
additionally include abortion in instances when the patient’s health was at risk, as well as in 
cases of rape and incest, the VA made a very narrow but critical change to the rule that aligned 
with other federal policies. After the 2022 rule changes were adopted, only a small number of 
abortions were provided at the VA. However, over 70% of abortions provided in the first year 
were because of a threat to the woman's health, showing the urgent need for this expansion to 
provide needed health care.4 Proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31 would rescind this careful expansion 
and the recognition that veterans and their families need access to abortion care in specific 
scenarios through their trusted health care provider, the VA. This change will result in worse 
health outcomes for VA and CHAMPVA beneficiaries. 
Without the ability to clearly treat patients who need abortion care to preserve their long-term 
health and only the ability to provide abortion care, at least for some VA patients, when “the life 
of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term,” physicians will be forced 
into difficult situations where they will have to determine, often under time pressure and facing a 
sick patient, whether they are legally allowed to provide appropriate and critical care to their 
patients. Notably, for veterans themselves, physicians’ ability to provide life-saving care is even 
less clear, as the rule fails to include clear language. Similar situations have already arisen under 
state laws that either only have a life exception or are unclear.  For example, in one case, a 
woman who was six weeks pregnant was diagnosed with breast cancer and could not start 
treatment until the pregnancy was ended but could not get an abortion in her state because it 
would have been considered “health” saving instead of “live saving.”5 This patient had to travel 
to another state to end her pregnancy and the delays associated meant that it was several months

before she could begin chemotherapy, giving the cancer an opportunity to spread.6 In another 
case, a woman who needed a liver transplant, typically required by individuals in cases of liver 
failure or with liver cancer,7 had matched with a donor and was set to begin her transplant when 
it was discovered that she was early in an unplanned, unwanted pregnancy. Despite the obvious 
need to preserve her health with this complex, planned operation, the hospital canceled the 
transplant rather than end the pregnancy to move forward with the procedure￼  In some 
situations, health care providers may be forced to turn patients away or delay care until the 
patient’s condition worsens to ensure they are clearly only providing abortion care if the patient’s 
life is at risk. These types of delays, when implemented at the state level, have been found to 
produce significant negative health consequences, such as obstetric complications, hemorrhage, 
infection, and in a few cases, death.8,9  
B. The proposed rule creates unnecessary barriers to health care.   
Again, under the previous administration, the VA recognized that abortion services should at 
least be covered and provided in cases of rape and incest and that VA policy should allow for 
abortion counseling when the procedure cannot be performed at a VA facility. This proposed 
rule also rescinds these narrow expansions. Unfortunately, a significant number of female 
veterans have experienced sexual assault and may need to access this care.10 There are nearly 
400,000 veteran women of reproductive age living in RFA member states, who already face high 
risk of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), suicide, and sexual trauma.11 If this policy is

adopted, after traumatic instances of rape or incest, these women will not be able to seek this 
care at their trusted medical provider, the VA.  
For some of the 4.4 million veterans who live in rural areas and have few alternatives for health 
care providers or for those who cannot afford to arrange care for their children, get time off 
work, or pay for travel, this rule change could mean the difference between being able to make 
their own difficult decision after a traumatic incident or being forced to carry a pregnancy 
resulting from rape or incest to term. Moreover, without the ability to receive counseling and 
referral to other health care options, many women may not even be provided the information 
needed to seek care outside of the VA. The proposed rule’s prohibition on abortion counseling 
would create a cruel barrier to health care for veterans and their families. 
C. The proposed rule shirks the federal government’s responsibility to care for our 
nation’s veterans. 
More than 9 million veterans receive their health care from the VA, and women veterans of 
reproductive age represent the largest growing cohort of new VA patients.12 The federal 
government has a responsibility to provide them with the full range of necessary health care 
services when they return to civilian life. Under the proposed rule, pregnant patients who are the 
victims of rape or incest or are in situations where the pregnancy threatens their health but is not 
imminently life-threatening would be forced to seek care outside of the VA system. They would 
have to pay out of pocket or rely on the states that support a full range of reproductive health 
care to help pay for that care. Further, due to the lack of clarity for the veterans’ care specifically, 
some patients facing life-threatening situations may be unable to get the care they need, with 
disastrous consequences. 
Abortion services often exceed $500, increasing in cost with delays to care, and 43% of women 
of reproductive age do not have the savings to cover these costs.13 Without coverage or savings 
to pay for these services, some patients may forgo needed care. RFA states are committed to 
providing abortion access to all who need it to prevent this from happening. However, this 
proposed rule comes at a time when state governments are facing unprecedented strain on their

budgets, leaving limited resources.14 RFA states are deeply concerned by the federal 
government’s proposed rollback of reproductive health care access to which veterans, and their 
families, are entitled. Proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31 betrays the federal government’s 
responsibility to provide critical health care services to veteran families. 
RFA strongly opposes RIN 2900-AS31 and all efforts to restrict access to reproductive care for 
our nation’s veterans. As a coalition of 23 governors, the RFA firmly stands to ensure that access 
to the full range of health care services, including reproductive care, is available for every person 
served by the VA in the states they govern. 
 
Respectfully submitted,  
 
Christina Chang  
Executive Director
